title: Retrieval evaluation and ranking denominators

key_terms.Recall at k: The fraction of the known relevant documents that appear in the first k distinct results.
key_terms.Reciprocal rank: One divided by the position of the first relevant result, averaged across queries as MRR.
key_terms.nDCG: Discounted cumulative gain at k divided by the ideal DCG from sorting known relevance grades.
key_terms.Judgment pool: The set of judged documents; relevant documents outside it can change recall and the ideal ranking.

outcome: Evaluate retrieval separately from answer quality with explicit relevance grades, duplicate handling and unjudged-document policy.
verification: An ideal top two still misses one relevant document, a miss scores 0 for recall, reciprocal rank and nDCG, duplicate and unjudged documents are rejected, and an empty relevant set reports missing values instead of 0 or 1.

exercises.title: Separate recall from nDCG
exercises.task: Explain why case A has nDCG 1 but recall 2/3.
exercises.expected: An ideal top two still omits one relevant document.
exercises.answer: nDCG evaluates the quality of the available ranking positions. Recall asks what fraction of all known relevant documents was retrieved.

reasoning.approach: Read case A: gold grades `{"a": 3, "b": 2, "c": 0, "d": 1}`, ranking `["a", "b", "c"]`, cutoff 2. Count relevant documents (grade above 0) and see which appear in the top two.
reasoning.why: Three documents are relevant: a, b and d. The top two are a and b, so recall is 2 / 3. nDCG compares the top two with the ideal top two, grades 3 and 2, which is exactly what was returned, so nDCG is 1. The missing d does not fit in two positions anyway.
reasoning.pitfall: Expecting nDCG 1 to mean everything relevant was found is the mistake. nDCG at k only judges the k available slots. A cutoff smaller than the relevant set guarantees recall below 1 even for a perfect ranking.
reasoning.verify: Worked case A asserts the result equals `{"recall": 2 / 3, "mrr": 1.0, "ndcg": 1.0}`. Raising k to 3 with `d` in third place would make recall 1.

exercises.title: Return no relevant hit
exercises.task: Rank only the irrelevant document at depth 1.
exercises.expected: Recall, reciprocal rank and nDCG are 0.
exercises.answer: Zero is meaningful here because relevant documents exist in the judged corpus but none was retrieved.

reasoning.approach: Call `retrieval_metrics(["b"], {"a": 1, "b": 0}, 1)`. The single returned document has grade 0, and one relevant document, `a`, exists.
reasoning.why: Recall is 0 / 1 = 0. No relevant hit appears, so the first-hit position is `None` and reciprocal rank is 0. DCG is 0 while ideal DCG is positive, so nDCG is 0. Each zero is a real failure on a query where success was possible.
reasoning.pitfall: Treating these zeros like the missing values in exercise 5 would remove a real failure from the mean. The distinction is whether any relevant document exists in the judgments; here one does.
reasoning.verify: The reference asserts the result equals `{"recall": 0.0, "mrr": 0, "ndcg": 0.0}`. Swap to `["a"]` with k 10 and confirm nDCG is 1.

exercises.title: Repeat a document
exercises.task: Put the same relevant ID in two result positions.
exercises.hint: Evidence identity is part of the ranking contract.
exercises.answer: Counting duplicates as new hits can inflate recall or distort position metrics.

reasoning.approach: Call `retrieval_metrics(["a", "a"], {"a": 1, "b": 0}, 2)`. The guard compares `len(set(ranking))` with `len(ranking)` and raises.
reasoning.why: A retriever that returns the same relevant ID twice would earn DCG credit at positions 1 and 2. If recall counted list entries rather than distinct IDs, it could exceed 1. Rejecting duplicates keeps every metric tied to distinct documents.
reasoning.pitfall: Deduplicating inside the metric seems kind, but it hides a retriever bug. A system that wastes slots on duplicates should be fixed upstream, and its effective depth reported, not scored as if its list were clean.
reasoning.verify: The reference includes `(["a", "a"], 2)` in the invalid cases and fails with `Invalid ranking accepted` if it passes.

exercises.title: Add an unjudged document
exercises.task: Return a document absent from the relevance map.
exercises.hint: Unknown relevance is not proven irrelevance.
exercises.answer: A separate assessment or a declared missing-judgment policy is needed before comparing systems fairly.

reasoning.approach: Call `retrieval_metrics(["x"], {"a": 1, "b": 0}, 1)`. Document `x` has no grade, so the check `d not in relevance` raises `Unjudged document`.
reasoning.why: Unjudged documents are common when a new retriever surfaces items the original assessors never saw. Treating them as irrelevant penalizes the new system for novelty, and treating them as relevant rewards it without evidence.
reasoning.pitfall: Filling missing grades with 0 is the usual shortcut. It biases comparisons in favor of the system whose results were used to build the judgment pool, which is usually the older one.
reasoning.verify: The reference includes `(["x"], 1)` in the invalid cases. Either judge the new document or declare a policy (such as condensed lists that skip unjudged items) and apply it to every system.

exercises.title: Empty relevant set
exercises.task: Evaluate a query for which every judged document has grade 0.
exercises.expected: Recall and nDCG are reported as missing.
exercises.answer: Report the affected query count and its interpretation instead of silently mixing undefined scores into a mean.

reasoning.approach: Call `retrieval_metrics([], {"b": 0}, 1)`. No judged document has a positive grade, so the function returns `None` for all three metrics before computing anything.
reasoning.why: Recall divides by the number of relevant documents, here 0, and ideal DCG is also 0. Both ratios would be 0 / 0. Returning `None` keeps the query visible as undefined instead of assigning a misleading number.
reasoning.pitfall: Filling `None` with 1 (nothing to find, so perfect) or 0 (nothing found) changes the mean depending on how many such queries exist. A test set with many empty-relevance queries could then swing averages without any change in retrieval quality.
reasoning.verify: The reference asserts `retrieval_metrics([], {"b": 0}, 1)["recall"] is None`. In a report, give the count of such queries and exclude them explicitly from each average.

exercises.title: Preserve target weights
exercises.expected: They can differ without a coding error.
exercises.answer: The weighting rule defines whose query distribution the result represents; it should be shared by every compared retriever.

reasoning.approach: Take two queries with nDCG 1.0 and 0.5. Average them with equal weights, then with traffic weights such as 0.9 and 0.1.
reasoning.why: The equal average is 0.75 and the traffic-weighted average is 0.9 times 1.0 plus 0.1 times 0.5 = 0.95. Both are correct arithmetic. They answer different questions: typical query quality versus quality experienced by the average request.
reasoning.pitfall: Comparing retriever A's traffic-weighted mean with retriever B's equal-query mean is the mistake. The gap would come from the weighting, as in eval-005, not from the retrievers.
reasoning.verify: Recompute both averages for each retriever with the same weight vector, and confirm the difference between retrievers is reported under one stated weighting.
